Of course.  There are three main components to a GPS system:

A receiver that receives signals from satellites
An algorithm that processes those signals to generate location data
A user’s device that displays the resultant data

A receiver does the most work.  Once the signal is received, the receiver matches the signal’s frequency to that of a signal that is coming from a satellite in orbit around the Earth.  The receiver sends out a signal of its own in the direction that the satellite is pointed in, and the satellite re-responds with its signal, which contains information about the receiver’s position. The process of deriving position from signal is known as “定位” (lìdìng) or “定位测量”, and it can often be simplified to a simple formula:

Distance = Frequency X Time

Time is the time elapsed since the signal was received.  The satellites orbit the Earth, and the receiver also orbits the Earth.

This is the basic idea, but it’s also important to understand that, in order to get a precise position, the receiver has to keep track of the time it took for the signal to reach it, and the time it took for the signal to travel back to the satellite.  Both times have to be taken into account, or the position derived could be very inaccurate.  When the receiver was last on Earth, it was likely that there was a significant amount of time where it would not have been able to receive the signal, especially if the receiver was close to the equator.  To avoid this, the receiver tracks the time of other satellites in the system, in order to estimate the time it took for the signal to reach it, and the time it took for the signal to travel back.  If the receiver is off the equator, this is less accurate, but still a useful approximation.  This tracking is done using data from other satellites, especially the ones that are closest to the Earth.  As more satellites are added to the system, the accuracy of the estimate improves.

Once the receiver has a location, it uses this location to define a “region of interest” (ROI) around the sender.  This is the area of the world that the sender is in, and this is used to get the distance and speed of the sender, which are the two parameters that affect the accuracy of a position estimate.  The sender knows the location of the receiver, and the receiver also knows the location of the sender.  They are then able to use the formula above to get the position of the sender, and the distance from the sender to the receiver.

The region of interest is defined using a formula of its own:

Region of Interest = Distance of Sender + Speed of Sender X Time elapsed since Last Contact

This formula defines a “region of interest” (ROI) to be the area around the sender.  The formula doesn’t really get into the calculations used to define the ROI, but you should be aware that the time that has passed since the last time that the signal was received and the time that it took for the signal to get to the sender must both be taken into account, and that the time elapsed since the last contact is used to estimate the length of the channel between the sender and the receiver.  In practice, most GPS devices will use “Free-space optical” as their term for this channel.  The method requires a high degree of accuracy, and is expensive to implement and maintain. In the GPS device that I have access to, the ROI definition is:

ROI = (Distance of Sender + Speed of Sender X Time elapsed since Last Contact) X Time Since Last Contact

Where the time since last contact is an estimate of the time elapsed since the signal was received.  The system itself tracks this value, and the device calculates the time since last contact based on the amount of time that has elapsed since the last time the signal was received, and the amount of time elapsed since the last contact.

The time since last contact is how long it took for the signal to travel from the sender, and to the receiver, and this value can give an indication of how accurate the position estimate is, or how fast the location is changing.  The longer this value is, the more accurate the position is.  This information is sent back to the GPS receiver by the satellite, and so it can either be downloaded immediately from the device, as a status message, or it can be used to further refine a position estimate.  Using this information can have a great effect on the accuracy of the position estimate, since any position changes can be ascribed to the time since last contact.
